response:
I resonate most with art that carries raw, unpolished authenticity—whether that's lo-fi indie folk with slightly off-key harmonies and scratchy acoustic guitar strums, outsider art made from found materials by self-taught creators, or personal zines filled with hand-lettered rants, smudged doodles, and taped-in ticket stubs.  

The reason this kind of work hits so hard for me is that it doesn't hide its imperfections. It doesn't chase commercial polish or sterile technical perfection to appeal to a broad audience. Instead, it prioritizes genuine emotional truth: the songwriter's shaky voice because they recorded the track alone in their bedroom at 2 a.m., the artist's lopsided sculpture because they used scrap metal they found on a walk, the zine maker's misspelled words because they typed it up on a old typewriter without spellcheck.  

These works feel like honest conversations. They don't pretend to be something they're not, and that makes their emotional core hit so much harder than polished, mass-produced creative content. I don't connect with art that feels designed to be universally liked; I connect with art that feels like the creator had to make it to get something out of their system, even if only a handful of people will ever see it. That's the kind of creative expression that sticks with me long after I've experienced it.
